utterances.text: And if we can just scroll to the bottom and perhaps go to the second page. I'm just asking you to look at it. This is a true and accurate copy of the materials that you reviewed as of February 2008 in connection with your testimony here today; correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: It appears to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, since February of 2008, were you provided additional materials or documents to further assist in your review and analysis of the scientific evidence that's been heard in this case?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Share with us what that is, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: I have been sent the testimony of other experts who have testified in a scientific capacity. I have also been given additional materials relating to a demographic study that was done in, I believe, 2005 for the OTP relating to the combination of the missing persons list with a 1991 Bosnian census. And a few other isolated materials, I can't recall off.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And since your arrival here at the Hague approximately a week or ten days ago, you've also met with me on a couple of occasions?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we have gone through some of that material, correct, as well as your report?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, what I'd like to ask you next is have you reviewed any outside materials other than those that you've just identified that are not listed in your report, such as textbooks, articles or other information that would have assisted you in formulating the opinions that you have identified in your report or will soon identify?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Share with us what those other materials were, if you will?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Many of them are included in the bibliographies that run through my report, so when I specifically referenced any one particular article or outside source, it will be referenced and identified within my report and the citation for the reference itself is provided at the end of each section.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you give, obviously, the source and the cite that you've relied on; correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You've also written, yourself, several articles, as you've shared with us. Did you write any specifically in connection with Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Specifically with Srebrenica there was one, there are a variety of other articles that do include a large sample size from Bosnia of which Srebrenica victims comprise a significant portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask about two specific reports to see if you've reviewed them. Can we have 2D70 brought up in the screen, please. It's 2D70. And Doctor, as that is being brought up just for you to see it, it's actually what's been to referred to commonly here as the San Antonio Report and I just have a couple of questions in connection with that. Obviously, the first one being have you had an opportunity to review the report that we've coined as the San Antonio Report, 2D70?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: I had an opportunity to read it in the past week.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Prior to the past week, did either Mr. Meek or myself give you a copy of this report or ask you to utilize it in formulating any of your opinions?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd also like to ask you with respect to Dr. Chester Elliot Moore III, I believe. Are you familiar with him?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What is his profession?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: He is also involved in forensic anthropology at the -- what is known as the JPAC, the joint military agency that's responsible for the identification of war missing in the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if I can show you with the Court's permission and court clerk's assistance 2D535, which is our proposed 92 bis statement. It's a rule of procedure here so you need not worry about that. We are waiting for Dr. Moore to provide us with an authorised and notarized statement. He has given us this. Have you had an opportunity to review Dr. Moore's report, if you will?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: In the past week I've read this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Prior to that you had not; correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, in looking at these materials that you've reviewed and relying on the various articles that you've examined as well as written, the updated materials that you've identified for us, the San Antonio Report as well as Dr. Moore's recent statement, have you relied on those documents and those articles in order to assist in formulating the opinions that you hold in connection with the task that you were assigned?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's turn to your report, Dr. Komar, if we may. That's 2D534, for the record. If we can have that brought up as well. Doctor, I think we have in front of us document 2D534. Can you just identify it for us, please?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: It was a witness statement I was asked to prepare in February of this year that would summarize some of the contents of my testimony here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, can you just walk us through briefly your report and we'll get into the details and some of the opinions that you hold as well as the basis of those opinions, can you just walk through it and I may try to assist you. I think it's broken down in five separate sections; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just for general purposes, it's broken down, I think, into your understanding and opinions you may hold with respect to ICMP and the DNA-based identification which would be one.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I apologise -- the next one is the MNI which is the minimum number of individuals; correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Then you discuss briefly Mr. -- or Dr. Lawrence's autopsy reports?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You discuss further the issue of, as you've identified it or as they have identified it, "robbing or rob"?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then finally you identify a group which is commonly or referred to in your discipline as social group identification?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, we are not going to go through each and every one of these but I would like to highlight two or three of these items in your report and to further obtain your opinions in connection with that. But before I do that, I'd like to ask you: Is your report current as it stands now, the one that you generated in February of 2008, in light of the additional material that you reviewed and relied upon or would you like to make any supplemental additions to it?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Based on the material I've had the opportunity to review particularly since I have arrived here, I would offer amendments to the report as questioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, before we go and delve into the report in detail, are you familiar with some of the scientists and anthropologists and archeologists and pathologists and DNA scientists that testified in this case, I know you've read their testimony but do you know them on a personal or professional basis?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Yes, it's a pretty small community and most of us have worked together at some point or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So when we go through this, obviously they are professionals as well, we are not asking to you render any criticisms of them personally because they are obviously doing the job that they were requested to, but we will go through some of that. These are certainly your colleagues, are they not?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And from time to time you see them on an exhumation and other times you may see them several years later; correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Correct or at professional functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Professional conferences?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Let's go through, if we may, the first section of your -- my outline and your report which deals with the MNI because, I think, since you were assigned that task initially, it might be most reasonable to start at that point. Tell us, generally speaking, although you mentioned -- describe what MNI is and you looked at various reports from, for example, Dr. Wright and Dr. Lawrence; correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And Dr. Baraybar?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Mr. Baraybar, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Baraybar, I'm sorry. And Mr. Manning; correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You've read their testimony in connection with that?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell us briefly, have you based upon a reasonable degree of anthropological and scientific certainty formulated an opinion having reviewed those materials as well as their testimony in connection with what they were trying to convey with respect to MNIs?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what is that?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Essentially as I understand a review of the material, there are two specific sources or separate sources upon which people are making assessments as to MNI, or how they are calculating or estimating MNI. Based on my review of that, there are some methodological deficiencies with the means by which these MNIs are calculated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'll try to just flush that out. You examined that and when you said -- when you identified generally the people, we were talking about the individuals who rendered testimony in this Court and people who have issued reports in connection with that topic MNI; correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: I guess I prefer to speak to their work product rather than the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Of course. That's exactly what we are evaluating. We are not addressing them personally, but I meant if we were going to highlight without going over their names again, Mr. Baraybar, Mr. Manning, Dr. Lawrence and Dr. --

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Dr. Wright?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Wright, thank you. Now, you say to make the assessments as to MNI, the process of making an assessment in connection with MNI, and I think you gave it to us in the latter half of your answer, is the actual methodological process; correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: It requires the application of a methodology to generate the estimate which is the goal of the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I'm correct, you would take this methodology and then you would do the analysis in order to reach a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, what was the methodology or what application of what methodology was used to generate an estimate?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: In my review of the material, it appears there's a sort of a time frame or a sequence of how this is done. The first reference I can find to a scientific estimate of MNI occurs in Richard Wright's exhumation field reports from the late 1990s. 1998, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have the date, the 12th of May, 1999, if we can please have P666 up on the e-court, please. And just so the record is clear and I think we advise that my learned friend Dr. Komar does have the binders the hard copies on them and if she would be kindly permitted to utilize that because she's familiar with where she's placed them in the various binders, with the Court's permission, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any problems with that, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Other Defence teams, any problems? Absolutely no problem on our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, you mentioned that you examined or looked at the report by Dr. Wright which is the 12th of May, 1999, that we have identified as P666. And you say this is the first evidence or at least the first information that you were able to glean where the identification of the issue MNI raised itself; correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Of the materials I reviewed, this is the earliest mention of any attempt I see by anyone to calculate an MNI, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Where in his report does he attempt to calculate an MNI? I think it is the 12th of May, 1999. Take your time.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: I found it. There is --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And Doctor, I'm sorry, I'll let you answer the question. Just so that we can keep up with you, it's actually on the second page of his report under the summary findings; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: That's a conclusionary statement, so essentially it's mentioned several times in the context of the report. Within the body of the report, it occurs at a later section and in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, direct us so that we can follow your analysis here with respect to Dr. Wright's report. What page on this be Exhibit P666 should we ask the Court and --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's page 32 of Dr. Wright's report, I believe?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Correct. It's 245.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: ERN number, the last three, 245. Thank you. We have now the document before us, you have the hard copy in front of you. Can you share with us your opinion in connection with the conclusions or the issue that Dr. Wright was addressing in connection with MNIs and keeping in mind that your general opinion was that the methodology, I think as you put, was deficient, if I got you right?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: That's correct. Essentially, he does two separate things within the context of this estimate. One is an evaluation of the material actually recovered within the field season. The second is an estimate based on a statistical and mathematical statement as to the total number of individuals that is potentially represented by the graves identified in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, why do you believe that that methodological evaluation or method utilized was deficient?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: In what is known as the SOP or the standard operating procedure of Mr. Wright's report, he identifies the fact that the purpose of the field exhumation is not to do analysis of the remains. It's a very clear statement within the body of the report on several occasions that there will be because of the conditions in the field, no attempt to actually analyse or understand the remains as they are being removed. It's an assessment of the grave. So essentially, to later indicate the number of individuals, he himself earlier in his report indicates that he is not doing sufficient analysis at that time and prefers that the work be done later in the morgue which is completely appropriate for these kind of circumstances. The number of individuals he offers at this point is more a statement of the number of body bags that were removed and by his own admission, that that necessarily does not represent an individual for that initial boxed or tabled statement of the number of individuals per site.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that was the methodology aspect of it. With respect to his conclusions that we see on the next page, page 33, am I correct that Dr. Wright simply in this report took a number and then from an average that they have exhumed and then just multiplied it by an estimate of 21 unexhumed graves and he came up with what was identified at that time as the first MNI or the early MNI?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: That's a correct assessment of the later half of that assessment. Essentially what he argues is that if you take the graves that have been done to date and use what he himself admits is not a definitive estimate of the numbers of individuals in it, you create an average and times it by what he believes to be the potential number of unexcavated graves. He produced what is essentially only an arithmetic statement as to what he believes the number of individuals represented is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let's just go back to the methodology again. Just share with us what your opinion is and why you think that the methodology utilized as reflected in this May 12th, 1999, report was deficient or defective?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: If you break it down again into these two components, let's start with the idea that we are actually counting the people coming out of the ground. Professor Wright himself acknowledges that they were not doing sufficient analysis at the scene to be able to create this number. He supplements the number with a report from Visoko. So essentially, he is including in this number some degree of subsequent analysis that was carried out in the morgue at a later date in Visoko. Not in and of itself erroneous or problematic other than if you then subsequently go to some of the autopsy reports coming out of Visoko as to how individuals were being defined both in the field and in autopsy.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just describe for me what you mean by not doing sufficient analysis at the scene. I mean, what were they not doing? I know as a general term what it means but if you could just, from an anthropological and forensic anthropologist standpoint, just help us have a better understanding in our mind as to what it is they should have been doing and then what it is they did not do based on that?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: In subsequent excavations that were done both in Bosnia and ultimately in other similar circumstances in the world, it's been understood particularly in graves that are in any way compromised, say secondary graves, graves with a great deal of settling, in which the individuals contained within are decomposed and are no longer articulated, therefore recognisable as defined human beings; they are no longer fleshed, they are no longer discrete units. There is not agreement both within these reports and within the anthropological community as to how we begin to define what constitutes a body. So at what point are we calling portions of an individual a body and at what points are we then subdividing that individual into what becomes known as body parts or miscellaneous or general elements. Professor Wright, within the context of his report, gives a vague and insufficient definition of how these determinations were being made.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And as a result of your opinion and analysis on this, you find that this report is suspect, if I can use that term?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object. This is manifestly leading and I think it's been going on for a while. I haven't objected but I think at this point I will start to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you wish to comment, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or do you wish to rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, I will rephrase it but I don't understand the point that it's been going on for a while. And if he can draw my attention, I would certainly invite him to show me one question where, other than a couple that I thought were for the sake of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's give that. Just rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, in connection with the opinion that you have in respect to this first report on MNIs, other than it it's methodologically deficient, do you have any other opinions based on a reasonable degree of forensic certainty, anthropological forensic certainty?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: While there is precedent for how the initial table is presented, the attempt to then establish a mean and to then extrapolate that across a number of graves that by Professor Wright's own admission in subsequent years did not yield bodies is fundamentally flawed. That is not acceptable practice. It is not a valid and scientifically appropriate way to estimate the number of individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, in your prior -- just moments ago you discussed various things like articulation and body bags, and are you familiar with the concept of disassociation and re-association?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Just share with us what that means.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Disassociation or disarticulation is the notion that the body is made up of a series of elements, some of which are preserved longer in the archeological record than others specifically, the bones, and that as the soft tissues decompose the body literally begins to fall apart or disassociate. The process of re-association is the scientific examination of isolated elements with the goal of essentially reconstituting the integrity of a body. You are literally trying to put someone back together.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And because you mentioned body bags in Professor Wright's statement or report that he provides, did you find any evidence of attempts at re-association or re-articulation?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: No. He makes it clear that in the field that was not the goal of what they were doing, so he makes the argument that because of the conditions at the time, it was not appropriate to try and reassociate people. He preferred that that be done within the context of the morgue during later analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you have an opinion as to whether or not that was reasonable to later have that re-association or re-articulation be performed at the morgue?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: That's common practice, and there's nothing inappropriate about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I agree. I just wanted to cover that. Now, did you see if there was some of the -- this scientific evidence that was brought forward at the morgue, whether there were efforts, specifically if we can just focus on this report for the time being and date of this re-articulation or re-association of body parts with bodies.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: If my understanding of the reports is correct, there is a subsequent analysis that was done at a later time. If the report that I'm -- was shown in reference is a direct relation to that, there was not an attempt at re-association, and in fact, what there was a decision by the lead pathologist to simply evaluate the body bags as they were received and to do things such as estimate the number of traumatic injuries and/or cause of death by body bag rather than by individual or even individual body part.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, given your testimony that that could have been done on the field, the re-association, re-articulation, and it's acceptable to defer that to the morgue, do you have an opinion based upon a reasonable degree of anthropological certainty whether or not the failure or having no evidence of it, that not being done at the morgue, do you have an opinion based on that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The objection is that I don't believe that the witness has stated that this could have been done in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I could clarify that with her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I just thought it was a presumption -- and I didn't mean to be presumptuous, but I'll clear it up with her. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then we are going to leave it in your hands. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Komar, is this re-articulation, did the anthropologist and the scientists who were actually on the field, did they have a capacity to be able to perform the re-articulation or re-association prior to the body or body bag being placed in the morgue?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: They had a standard operating procedure as defined by Professor Wright that they were not to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I'm not asking you that, and thank you for that. Is there capability from a scientific standpoint to accomplish such a task?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Re-association can essentially be done at any point that the remains can be evaluated appropriately. If field conditions exist, and I have done it and I've seen others do it, that the remains can be evaluated properly, it has been done and can be done in the field. There was a decision made by Professor Wright that that would not be done here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I understand. We are just saying in the remote possibility under certain circumstances, does it ever exist that an anthropologist or an archeologist or a pathologist are able to perform that scientific re-association or re-articulation. I think you've answered. Now, to go back to my question before I was interrupted, given your testimony that although back -- Professor Wright had a standard operating procedure not to do this and now learning from your review of the materials that at the morgue they also did not do that, do you have an opinion based upon a reasonable degree of forensic anthropological certainty as to whether or not that failure of not doing this re-articulation being done at the morgue was proper or reasonable?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: If -- it is not consistent with the standards that we recognise today.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: I'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that's what we are asking you for, and that's the applicable scientific standards that should have been utilized at the time and that are applicable today. Was there a deviation from those standards of acceptable practice from an anthropological point not having done this at the morgue?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: It calls into question the veracity of the numbers that are presented here. It -- there can be an argument, debate on both sides as to whether resources, time, personnel allow for everything that can be done to be done. This would be something that I personally would argue is a necessary step in the proper analysis of the remains. Had I been responsible for this particular site, I certainly would have attempted it; I certainly would have addressed it to a far more exhaustive level than was done here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Again, Doctor, we are not sitting here and trying to say that Professor Wright or any of the other scientists who were involved in here did anything purposefully wrong or unreasonably wrong. We are just trying to get a better appreciation for how much or how valid or, as you say, how reliable or unreliable some of the data that's been provided are. That's what we're trying to examine here. Thank you for that. With respect to that Professor Wright, do you have any other opinions or would you like to identify any other areas where you find that the report with respect to the MNI was methodologically deficient?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Again, this mathematical statement of estimate is not, in my opinion, a valid scientific exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And That's what we see on the second page, which I think was 33 of his report, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: I think it's the bottom of 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And I think if you look on the next page that, in fact, he summarily concludes the first estimate of an MNI, correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: That's correct. He essentially goes through the mathematical statement and draws a conclusion at the end of page 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. I just want to make sure we are all on the same page. Any other opinions in connection with this 12th May 1999 Professor Wright report that you would like to share with us?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: With regard to MNI?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: No, not at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We're just going to focus on MNI and not some of the other stuff for at least this portion of your questioning. Now, the next report that you looked at with respect to MNIs were Dr. Lawrence's autopsy report, correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: In only a general sense in that he does not expressly answer the question of MNI because of the methodology he chose to employ in his analysis. So he doesn't make an expressed statement of MNI; therefore, I cannot derive an express statement of MNI from his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you derive from reading his report what that methodology is that he utilized?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Again, he chose to analyse and evaluate the remains, not through an attempt to re-articulate or define individuals but, rather, an attempt to understand the number of traumatic injuries or cause of death attributable to any one body bag. By doing that, it presupposes or assumes that more definition or more analysis was done in the field than is actually the case here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like -- and I forgot to ask you this during your background experience. You also -- you mentioned Kosovo, obviously, but you also worked in the Foca area in the former Yugoslavia, correct, on exhumations, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you were involved there as a hired forensic anthropologist who assisted the recovery and uncovering and exhumation of various grave sites, correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that was in what year, just so we can have a ...

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Foca was 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what I'd like to do is to look at the next report that I believe that you examined, and that was the -- Mr. Baraybar's December 8th, 1999, report, and I think it's P559. If we could kindly have that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... and the break will be at 12.30 as scheduled.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Komar, as you are finding the document, just so the record's clear and my learned friends can follow along, Dr. Baraybar actually has two specific reports, and I'm going to try to break it down so that we can look at each. It's the December 8th, 1999, report as identified, which is P559, but also the January 2004 report, which is soon -- when we get through it is 2477. So I'd like first if you would be kind enough to walk me through the December 8th, 1999, report.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: It's essentially what's known as a summary report of a field exhumation, so he's describing the field season as a whole, and what he's addressing specifically is the anthropological examination of the remains that take place after the field exhumation and during the autopsy phase of the analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What was -- I'm not sure if I understand you. What was the methodology that he used in connection with this field exhumation or field season as a whole as you call it?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: He is not addressing MNI in the field. He addresses it in the autopsy suite.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And what methodology does he use in the autopsy suite?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: He acknowledges that simple body count is not sufficient in that -- because you have disarticulation of the remains. It isn't as simple as simply counting bodies. At this point, what he chooses to do is essentially a standard, accepted protocol within anthropology that recognizes that individuals are represented by specific elements. So in other words, if you have 12 skulls, you must have at least 12 individuals who contributed those skulls to the analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the same can be said for the femur or the humerus, correct, the leg femur or -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: When we do these types of analysis, you can do them in a variety of ways: One, you can use unpaired or single bones, those bones that occur in the mid-line of the body, so say the breastbone or sternum, the skull, the jaw, the sacrum, for which you have one part. It runs along the mid-line. The alternative is to recognise that there are paired or bilateral bones; you have a right and a left. If you are going to do this kind of analysis with the paired bones, you must include the notion of side within your analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So right side or left side predominantly?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Was that ever done in connection with any of the reports - I know I'm deviating a little bit from the Baraybar report - in connection with a humerus or a femur?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: It's my understanding that was the core with modifications of the methodology he employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And which one did they utilise?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: It's difficult to tell from this report. There appears to be a combination of bones that are used. He frequently references the proximal femur, which is the portion of your thigh bone that connects with your hips. He also makes reference of pelvic bones, sternum, and other long bones, paired long bones.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Having reviewed the Baraybar report of December 8th, 1999, were you able to formulate an opinion as to a reasonable degree of certainty as to whether or not methodologically there were any flaws that you found?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: That methodology is described to that point as absolutely standard procedure. He makes two modifications to it that can challenge the validity of the ultimate results.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you share with us where those two modifications are that he makes which may challenge the validity of the result?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: The first -- essentially when we do this, we can also -- or he chooses to also look at what are known as variables. In this case he introduces two variables. The first is the sex of the individual as determined through anthropological examination; the second is the age of the individual as determined through anthropological examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So the reliance on sex and age are the two elements that you would consider to be variations or modifications in the methodology that was utilized?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Again, it's not unheard of that they are used. It's how they are used in this particular instance that is questionable.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Direct us, if you will, please, to the page on Baraybar's December 8th, 1999, report upon which you are referencing now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, and that is still on Exhibit P559. Thank you. And they only have an ERN number. They don't have a page number on the bottom, so I apologise for that. Doctor, once it's up on the screen, if you could just assist us and direct us where exactly that's addressed.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: He goes through his methodology fairly clearly and concisely by saying that initially the calculation begins with an assessment of this bone. So you establish what bone you are using to determine your MNI. If you have the most of your proximal right femur, then it makes sense and is appropriate to argue that if you have 54 right femora, you must have minimally at least the 54 individuals that contributed those femora to the analysis. It is possible you would have more; it is not physically possible to have less. That's appropriate. In the middle of that page in the second full paragraph, he introduces the notion of sex. How we determine sex anthropologically does not inherently follow how the remains were analysed to determine the MNI. So essentially, what happens is if you use, say, the sacrum or the sternum to establish your MNI to get your base count, there isn't necessarily a corresponding method that is accepted in the anthropological community that allows you to determine sex from those specific bones.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Again, I don't want to lead you on this, so am I understanding this correctly, because they are not using the proper bones or the -- evaluating or examining the proper bone, it would be hard-pressed for one to be able to make a conclusion in connection with sex? Am I as a layperson trying to -- I apologise for not understanding this a little better.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: What I would say is, essentially it appears that what they are examining either has to be relatively complete bodies, which is possible but does not necessarily reflect what is described in the report. So in other words, if I'm going to establish MNI using a sternum, there is no method by which I can then use that same sternum to determine whether it's a male or a female. The parts of the body you need to do that are either the pelvis, the skull, or metrically, through analysis of either the head of the humerus, how big the top of your arm is or the head of the femur. So if he chooses to use the proximal femora, it is possible to do some metric analysis to divide males from females. If he uses the other bones identified in this report, there is no accepted anthropological method that ties the idea of sex to those bones unless you presuppose that what he is examining or what the individuals are examining is close to a relatively complete body or that re-association has been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to there being a complete body or re-association in order to obtain a complete body, in the report there's no evidence that that -- or little evidence, if I may use that, to support that, correct? Strike that. I'll restate it. I'll restate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yeah, yeah, yeah. It's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is there any -- I'm sorry. Really, is there any evidence in the report to identify that there were complete bodies or re-association to complete bodies?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: I see no express evidence that that was done. You could also make the argument that if you had complete bodies, you have an MNI. You count the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand that. Thank you. Just briefly, and we have just a few minutes before our next scheduled break, which I'm sure you'll look forward to. With respect to the aspect of sex, is your opinion -- or what is your opinion now in connection with age? Because you've said these are the two modifications, one being sex, the other being age.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Again, it goes to the issue of the bone you use to establish MNI is not inherently the bone you would use to establish the age of the individual. So it presupposes that if you were going to use, say, a sternum, again, to establish your MNI, there is no method that then allows you to age that sternum in order to subdivide it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we can see the methodology as well as the analysis utilized by Mr. Baraybar in his December 1999 report on 00911541, correct? I mean, it's captioned "age," and presumably it's in that report that the methodology is described as well as on the next page where they render the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: On Table 3, he gives an express and explicit statement of the methods used to establish age, all of which are acceptable methods, all of which are perfectly relevant to establishing the age of an individual, but that those methods don't inherently apply to the bones that were used to establish the MNI. So unless you have relatively complete individuals, you are making analysis of separate or isolated or unreassociated bones.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think at this point we can all use a break, [indiscernible] more so, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Komar. Doctor, we were talking about little bit about the sex and age in the last session and I just wanted to follow up, if we may, on this section of age with respect to Baraybar's December 8, 1999, report. Are there any other opinions you have in connection with that and specifically, if I can direct your attention to the issue of or -- for example, is the age range too wide or do you find any other defects or deficiencies in that methodology utilized by Baraybar?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: It's not that the age ranges are too wide, they reflect the methodologies he is employing; it's that the age categories as they are defined don't inherently reflect the way we establish age. My most troubling, I guess, comments are the notion that we can separate a 17-year-old from an 18-year-old based on the methodology as they exist and particularly with relation to the bones they are talking about. I think it -- that there's significant overlap between the age categories as they are defined and particularly and in what can be defined or categorized as a crucial age category, this notion of the late teens early adulthood, I think it suggests a degree of specificity that is not reflected or that warranted by the methodology being employed; in other words, I would not argue that we can conclusively and unambiguously separate a 17-year-old from an 18-year-old.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I can just direct your attention to your report under section 2.2, and so you can assist me in understanding this section where you say the age and death calculation -- under 2.2. And again, it's on Dr. Komar's report which is 2D534, and we are looking under paragraph section 2.2, please.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just so I understand, what is this section dealing with, because I note that you do mention Baraybar in his 1999 report as well as his 2001 and 2004 reports. And you talk about the usage of the right or left femur, which we discussed, and then also you go on to say that none of the -- down below, I think in the sixth line, "However, none of the aging methods cited in Baraybar's protocol," and then you make reference to his three reports, "use the femur, ribs, et cetera, as the aging standard)." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: There's a separation of thought. None of the aging methods use the femur; in fact, it's ribs, [indiscernible] and teeth that are used as the standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's my understanding of it. I just wanted to clarify. So they are not using the femur which is the acceptable standard method, they are using the ribs?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: No, it's -- I'm not arguing that the femur is an accepted method. I guess if I have any comment regarding this it is that perhaps Jose Pablo Baraybar is not sufficiently clear in his methodology as to allow an outside individual to assess exactly what was being done. He makes sort of -- I don't want to use the word vague but tangential comments regarding the bones that he does or does not use in any particular site and it's completely acceptable to use different sets of remains for different sites. You are looking at each site in its toto and trying to determine what's your most common element. All of that is acceptable. What is not clear is how the relationship between -- how he makes the connection between the elements and material we look at in order to establish age and how that corroborates with the elements you would then use to establish MNI, that that connection is not clear in the report as it's written and it's not clear as someone who understands exactly what it is he's trying to do and how he's doing it, how he accomplishes what he claims to accomplish.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's see if Baraybar in his subsequent report makes it somewhat more clear. I direct your attention, if I may, to his January 2004 report which is P2477. Specifically, just so that we can follow along with you, I think we are going to highlight initially ERN number 03489048, which is where they discuss the MNI procedure.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But before we go there, Doctor as it's being placed, are there any other opinions or comments or thoughts that you would like to make in connection with the December 1999 report that you formulated here?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: I would sum it up by saying that there's a lack of clarity as to exactly how the connection is made between how age is established and how the MNI is calculated. He describes the two processes separately but fails make the connection other than that they are evaluating significant portions of remains and/or complete bodies, in which case MNI is not the question before the examiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now directing your attention to P2477, which should be on the screen, and we've asked that the specific number be placed on which is ERN 3 -- 03489048 and I think we also would need 47 on the screen at one point, I'm just giving a heads up. I think it actually starts on that prior page.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: It begins on what he's marked as page 3048 and continues through 049.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, having reviewed this report and based upon your experience, naturally, and education, did you form an opinion in connection with this report specifically as it relates to the MNI procedure that was utilized, that we see in Baraybar's January 2004 report?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Much of it is a duplicate of what has previously happened. There are significant improvements in this particular report in that he is far more specific for each site as to what he is using to establish MNI. Where again there can be some suggestion of a lack of clarity is, again, how the connection between, say, the right or left proximal femur which is overwhelmingly what he uses, connects to the notion of sex and age as was determined by what have to be considered individuals. If you are going to establish age and sex, you are essentially talking about something other than isolated elements. Whereas MNI essentially relates to this idea of isolated elements. You are trying to get an estimate of how many people are represented by the mismatch and collection of material that is left over in these disarticulated sites. And if I have a comment it is simply that it is not clear from the way it is written how he accomplished that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But this lack of clarity in the report, that goes to the, if I can use the term and I know we've discussed it briefly, one can't reasonably rely on this because there's no evidence to suggest that it was done properly or improperly. Would that be an appropriate way to say it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Same objection, Mr. President. It's, really, unconscionably leading in the circumstance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll restate the question, but really, I don't think it's necessary to say things such as these are unconscionable or -- but those are -- fine. If he needs to use those adjectives, that's fine. I don't think it was leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But in any event, Dr. Komar, with respect to the issue of lack of clarity that you discussed, what impact does that have for an objective or independent scientist such as yourself or others to evaluate the veracity or the credibility of the conclusions that are reached by Baraybar in his January 2004 report?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: While the individual methods and items he outlines are acceptable in isolation, I would have to suggest that in combination it is unclear how they accomplished this. Frequently, he uses -- creates examples to clarify the point, and it makes the point quite clear if a layman was reading this, where the connection is failed to be made is how it then translates into what he is actually looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that which he is actually looking at is what?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: A collection of -- again, a secondary or what he refers to as merged graves, this idea that there are some individuals who are still articulated, perfectly understandable in the circumstances, mixed with those who are disarticulated, and therefore that does pose a legitimate question to investigators, how do we figure out exactly how many people we are talking about here? Again, you know, in and of itself, introducing sex, introducing age is not unacceptable methodology; it is just not clear from how it's written and how it's presented how he makes the connection between isolated remains that he describes as forming the basis of his MNI and how those are then sexed and aged, absent any methodology that allows you to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Baraybar in his report on page 4 uses language such as the same logic applies for determination of sex, and in other parts he says the same logic is used for the application of determination of age. Can you share with us if his report identifies what logic he is actually utilizing in his methodology in order to reach those conclusions?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Essentially, the statement of logic that goes to MNI says that you can't have less than the people that are represented. If you have five right proximal femurs, you must have five people. He extends that logic to the idea of sex. If you have what is clearly a female femora and five right femora, then you would argue that you have what represent five male femora and one female femora, thereby raising the MNI to six. Even if you don't actually have an additional element, he is introducing the notion of sex as a way of further differentiating the individuals and further amplifying the estimate that basically -- and again, in and of itself, nothing wrong with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I actually like the word "amplifying the estimate" because I was going to use "inflated," but we'll go with your word "amplifying." So the net result is by using this methodology, although it's unclear, and by purportedly identifying this logic that they've utilized in determining age and/or sex, when you say there's an amplification, what do you mean? Is that an inflation or increase in the potential number of individual bodies or ...

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Inflation sounds like there's a purposeful statement to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: I would suggest that if -- what it potentially does is introduce bias, and a bias is a skewing of results in a particular direction. In this particular case, by introducing additional variables, inherently the skew is going to be for a higher number than a lower number.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, and I don't mean to impute anything negative to Baraybar or any of the other scientists here. With respect to, as you call it, amplification or higher numbers, can you detect as to whether or not that was reasonable in making a determination as to what the minimal number of individuals were in his 2004 or any of his other reports, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: In the 2004 report, he goes a step further in that he introduces what he calls an MMNI, which is a minimum -- minimal number of individuals. While he is certainly not the only person that has ever proposed that idea, what he uses it to introduce is the idea of hidden or invisible individuals. So what he is suggesting is that by his own methodology, he recognizes that there are certain individuals who are not captured within that system, so that -- what he is suggests is that simply counting the bones enough in these circumstances is not sufficient to identify the minimum number of individuals, that he argues you have to recognise the potentially individual -- or invisible individuals that could be counted as well. That -- that would have less acceptance in our community than a simple calculation of MNI.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. So -- and that was going to be my question. With this MMNI, is that widely a practice that forensic anthropologists would utilize or scientists in the field in determining MNI, or is that something that we see for the first time in this report of January 2004?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: I would in no way suggest he invented it. There are others who have invoked it. Again, we come down to the logic of how we makes the argument that you would count those individuals. It is appropriate and completely acceptable to identify the potential that there are people not being captured. He goes a step further and attempts to quantify that, and I don't know that I'm comfortable with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. In the report, did you find any evidence of, as you've identified it, the re-articulation or re-association of various body parts to bodies?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Within the context of this report, I don't see evidence of that; but to be fair, this report deals with MNI and not re-association.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, but in constituting or determining MNI or MMNI, would you know -- any of his other reports, do they address this re-association or re-articulation?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: I don't recall specific references to an effort to do it. I understand and have worked with Jose Pablo and know that his methodology frequently incorporates that. I don't see an express statement to that effect, and that just might be an artifact of how he wrote the report and not actually what happened in the field. I can't speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, because we've reached the 2004 period, although we are going to jump a little bit with the next report by Dean Manning, one of the investigators for the Prosecution, I wanted to ask you: Were you during the digs in Cancari and Liplje?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel and witness kindly asked not to overlap for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When you were involved in those two particular digs involving the Srebrenica area, how many scientists were involved in each or either one of those exhumations?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: There was an investigator who is not a scientist. There was the chief archeologist John Sterenberg [phoen], who was a scientist. There was myself as the osteologist; I had a graduate student with me. And then in addition to that, we had several local workers who assisted but I would not put in the category of scientist.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the investigator from the OTP who assisted or was present during the exhumation process?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Mike Hedley.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think you had identified him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And it's in your report and thank you. I just wanted to know if you recalled it. Now, if we can look at the next document that I'd like to review with you today here. Is the Dean Manning report, 3D261. And it's the June 8th, 2007, report. We are just waiting, Doctor, for the report to be brought up on the screen. Again, it's 3D261. Doctor, in preparation and in formulating your reviews and opinions in connection with the materials that you reviewed, is this also a report that you reviewed and analysed?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And can you tell me from the best of your recollection, just in general terms, what is the report and from whom? Other than the name Manning, do you know who he was and what role he played?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Dean Manning, my understanding, was an investigator for the ICTY. I believe he was a leader or team leader capacity and it represents a summary of the forensic evidence of mass graves to that point that relate to the Srebrenica investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, in your experience have you had investigators who would be involved in introducing MNIs?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: No. I was -- you specifically referenced Liplje and Cincari, I was expressly asked for an example of how this works by Mike Hedley to generate an estimate of MNI and I imagine within the context of his report hopefully he identified the source of that estimate and how I went about doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And in your opinion or do you have an opinion as to whether or not that was reasonable with what Mr. Hedley --

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Hedley.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Hedley?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Hedley, H-e-d-l-e-y.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm bad with last names. Mr. Hedley did, is that reasonable in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: It's common practice and very acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is the fact -- now you reviewed Mr. Manning's report, do you have an opinion whether or not it was appropriate for Mr. Manning to be introducing MNIs? But before you answer that question, you also reviewed his curriculum vitae that was attached as 2D541, if you remember. I know you won't remember the number but I think you looked at his CV; right?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: I understand your question, I would -- I don't know if I can ask you to rephase it but I'm a little uncomfortable with what you are asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You can. You can most certainly ask me to rephrase it, I think. I will rephase, if it permitted. Dean Manning we know is an investigator; we shared with you his curriculum vitae which is 2D541. What I'm asking in essence is: Do you have an opinion based upon a reasonable degree of scientific certainty as to whether or not it was appropriate for Dean Manning to be introducing MNI?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: There is nothing inappropriate about an investigator citing another source, a scientific source as to how -- if he chooses or she chooses to include an MNI in that report, it is appropriate and acceptable for them to identify the source of that report. If I had an opinion into this particular case, I think what makes me uncomfortable is that while Dean Manning identifies the DNA from the ICMP as the source of where his numbers are coming from, there is no specific scientific report that he is referencing for which those numbers are generated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When we review his report and some of the conclusions that he has reached, there's -- is there a basis for -- a reasonable basis as to how he comes to the conclusion for MNIs?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: The use of DNA as a source of generating an MNI is completely appropriate. If I have an objection to this particular report it is a sentence contained within it that transcends or - and purely my opinion - goes beyond the responsibilities and abilities of an investigator in that he makes a scientific assessment absent citing any scientific report he's generating this from, that disregards the anthropological source of MNI and replaces it with DNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just so the record's clear, and that's why I referenced his curriculum vitae, it's an investigator who does not have any scientific background or experience and that's really what you are referencing; correct? Because had he had some scientific experience or anthropological experience, would your opinion have still been the same?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: You are getting into degrees of what constitutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: -- I mean, just because somebody has a BA in anthropology doesn't necessarily qualify them make this assessment. If I can be clear for the purpose of the Court -- first of all, can I identify the sentence that I object to?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll get that. It's ERN 06106456 and it's the bottom of the third paragraph, I believe.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: What Mr. Manning states in his --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just give us a second if you don't mind. I'm sorry to interrupt you. Just so that we can follow along.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Okay. I was just going to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Page 2 of 23 of his report. And it's captioned "Number of individuals" in bold text and it's the third paragraph beneath that. We have it up now, Doctor, so can you focus which sentence or sentences that you are going to render an opinion on in connection with his report?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: It's the final sentence of the third paragraph which reads: "The results of this DNA analysis are therefore used in preference to the previously use anthropological MNI."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you this question, and forgive me for asking it. I think I know what it means but what does it mean to you as a scientist?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: That is a judgement call and a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think the question requires some clarification because the sentence refers to the substitution of this information in the context of the report that's being generated by Mr. Manning. It does not refer to the substitution of that information with respect to the scientific data upon which that report is based. And I think that my colleague can do more to clarify the question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It would please me to assist, if I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, you've heard what my learned friend has stated. Is there evidence of any scientific reliance that Dean Manning cites as to coming to his conclusion as to the MNI?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: If there is a report from ICMP that he is referencing, I have not seen it and I am not aware of it. And again, I don't wish to exceed what I'm being asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, obviously if there's a report I'm sure my learned friend would have tendered it and I'm sure he will show it to you when he has an opportunity to question. But given that you haven't seen that report, what is your opinion based upon a reasonable degree of certainty in connection with this?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: It is commonplace and appropriate for an investigator to reference a scientific report as the source of their information. If the purpose of the report is a summary of the overall investigation that it represents, it is appropriate and common practice for an investigator to reference a scientific report. What makes me uncomfortable about this particular event is it appears as though Mr. Manning has made a scientific decision that the anthropological MNI data that's been represented is being replaced by his interpretation of DNA analysis and the numbers generated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So what effect, if you are correct in how you read his statement, what effect is he saying the evidence of Dr. Wright and Jose Baraybar, what affect their reports and testimony has. He is saying that we have something else that's better and more improved and we shouldn't rely on their reports and others?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Again, I object. It's a leading question and furthermore, to the extent that it is my understanding that Mr. Ostojic wants the answer to that question, that is a question that he could have put to Mr. Manning at the time that he testified. I don't think it's appropriate for this witness to speculate as to what was intended by Mr. Manning when he drafted the report or what's written in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't think that I need to respond to that, that I could have or should have asked Mr. Manning. We've asked Mr. Manning many questions and I think the Court can go back and review that. I have a witness here who is qualified in order to render an opinion. This is obviously an investigator who had no anthropological or archeological or pathological experience whatsoever and he is now making a decision on behalf of the Prosecution that he is going to disregard some of the anthropological evidence. This anthropologist that's before us, I think has an opinion as to why and whether or not investigators should disregard and the value of anthropological MNI determination. So I think it's a fair question and it should be allowed that the witness answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First of all, I think that my colleague has misstated the record insofar as Mr. Manning's experience concerning the exhumations that were carried out in relation to this case. Second of all, I would point my colleague to the transcript, in particular on page 19002, which basically sets out what Mr. Manning did in relation to the preparation of this report. Specifically he says he used the data provided by ICMP and that is the basis of the -- that is the essence of the questions being put to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The next series of questions go to directly to ICMP because it naturally flows from that. The point being that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why don't you go there straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: She has an opinion in connection with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can ask her for her opinion along the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, what significance do you believe, and although you are an anthropologist -- not although, but you are an anthropologist, what evidence or how do you feel the use of anthropological science is in evaluating and determining MNI, do you think it's significant or insignificant?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: It is a recognised source of creating an estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And for how long has this been a recognised source of creating an estimate?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Throughout the history of anthropology. It is essentially a reliance on the logic that Mr. Baraybar references in his report, that if there are seven femora, there have to be at least seven people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it widely acceptable and considered reliable?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Manning seems to be moving away from the previously used anthropological scientific MNI estimates to what is commonly referred to DNA analysis; correct? Or so it seems?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Based on what is written.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let's talk a little bit about ICMP, if we can. Have you had any experience in dealing with that institution?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Share with us in what capacity and when.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: In 2001, I was contracted as a forensic anthropologist for the ICMP to assist in the exhumations jointly with the ICTY, specifically with the sites we discussed, Cincari 7 and Liplje 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with their SOP or standard operating procedures that may have been in existence at that time?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: I was not given any copies of SOPs at that time. I have since read the SOPs released by the ICMP within the context of this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We provided that to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know when those SOPs were actually formulated and implemented at the ICMP, by looking at the actual document?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: I can't speak to that. Most of them -- many of them are not dated which is standard operating procedure for a standard operating procedure. Given that my experience with the ICMP was limited to two months in 2001, I can't speak to what they did or did not do outside of that time-frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, your basic analysis and opinions that you render in connection with the ICMP DNA-based identification is actually found under subsection (1) of your report as well as various paragraphs 1.2, 3, 4, et cetera; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now we are going to cover that although we have 15 minutes. I don't know that we'll be able to accomplish the entire areas that I'd like to cover with you in connection with ICMP, but first and foremost, can you just help me understand the difference between matching rates and collection rates?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: The fundamental definition of those ideas?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So we can have a better appreciation when one take a matching rate and a collection rate?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: A matching rate is a statement of proportion of two populations that when compared to each other, either are concordant or disconcordant. If you have hundred of something and you compare it to a hundred of something else, a matching rate is a statement of how many of those two groups concur. Collection rates go to sampling strategies within a population. So it is first necessary to define your population; and secondly, it is important to establish what your sampling protocol and methodology is in order to determine whether or not your collection is representative of your population or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, and I know, and I apologise if I'm leading you on this, you ray viewed a two-page or so letter from Mr. Parsons from the ICMP, correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: I read a one-page memo from Dr. Parsons from the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now, was -- did you ever review -- because Mr. Manning in his report relies upon the DNA evidence in preference to the anthropological evidence, did you ever find or were you ever given a formal report from the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: I was not provided with that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So the only thing we have is the Dr. Parsons' report, and I don't have the date here in front of me, but I think it was in - I do have the date - the 30th of November 2007. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: 30 November 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I think it's been identified, just so that we can all follow along, as 1D703, but we will get back to that report in some detail. Now, in your report here you talk about a fundamental yet critical flaw in the logic that was used in order to create the estimated number of individuals missing from the Srebrenica area. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: In my report, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. And now, can you tell us why you find that there is a fundamental yet critical flaw in the logic, and help me understand, are you again addressing both the methodology and the analysis or, also, the methodology and analysis and conclusion when it comes in evaluating although obviously a very short -- I don't know that we can call it a report but a letter, if you will, and we'll talk about some of the contents of that letter a little later, this letter from Parsons dated 30th of November, 2007.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Just to be clear, the statement you referred to in my report references the ICMP statement from Parsons and not the report from Manning. The statement issued by Parsons called the ICMP Statement On Estimated Numbers appears to confuse the notions of collection rates and matching rates in the structure of the argument and ultimately the estimate he produces as a result of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay, and we'll address that. I just want to clear up one thing in your answer. You say, "Just to be clear the statement you refer to in my report references the ICMP statement from Parsons and not the report from Manning."
