And I just want to understand that because I don't know if I'm following, but Manning states that he has a preference, and now -- they are now going to essentially abandon the anthropological scientific analysis and this -- conclusions that were done in favour of the DNA. What report other than the Parsons 30th of November, 2007, report could Dean Manning possibly be relying on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think the question misstates the evidence and mischaracterizes the evidence. The document to which we were referred previously where Mr. Manning says that they are replacing or that he is replacing anthropological MNI with DNA MNI is a summary, and it's made in the context of the summary. It represents that what is depicted in the summary is this information as distinguished from the report that was previously filed. I think to characterize that as Mr. Manning substituting this information on a scientific level for the presentation to the Court I think mischaracterises the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask -- let me ask the doctor to clarify, and we're not trying to mischaracterize it at all. That's why we have Dr. Komar here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And Doctor, help walk us through that if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: It's actually rather clear. The date on Manning's report is June 8th, 2007. The Parsons report is produced November 30th, 2007. So Manning's report is written in advance of when Parsons' memo is created.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. So what is Manning relying on that he would make the statement that he has a preference to the DNA samples versus the anthropological scientific analysis that's been done up to that date in 2007?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: I don't know what report he is referring to. I haven't seen the report he is referring to. There is a release of information from ICMP in raw data form that I have seen that is concurrent with this particular event. There is no specific statement as to what he is referencing. He is very clear that it's coming from ICMP, and that's fair. I don't know where he gets the numbers or what allows him to make the statement that it is therefore preferential to the anthropological.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Does he identify it anywhere in his report, or its proclaimed that he does not, correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: I haven't found it. I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that my colleague is asking the witness to speculate as to these matters, and I think it's quite plain particularly, in light of the reference that I gave to the trial transcript in which Mr. Manning expressly states that he effectively -- and I'm quoting it; this is line 14 of page 919002, and it's a question put to Mr. Manning, "How did you reach this number, Mr. Manning, the number of 4017?" The answer is, "Your Honours, effectively I took the data provided by ICMP based on my knowledge of the graves and the types of codes used and the grid references, locations. I divided those figures into the relevant graves." That's how he arrived at the data. That's the source of the information that's relied on, and I think to make a representation to the contrary misstates the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Respectfully, I disagree because I think that is a misunderstanding. We're saying and I think Dr. Komar in her answer did refer to the raw data, and my question is simply other than that raw data that she's had an opportunity to review, was there another report or a formal report, or is the only thing that we see, although admittedly subsequent to Dean Manning's report in November 30th of 2007, this one page letter from Dr. Parsons, and all we are doing is narrowing it down. Dr. Komar has reviewed, I believe, the raw data and has herself reconfigured some of that, which we'll get to in a -- shortly, I hope. So I don't think we are mischaracterizing. I think they may have misunderstood what we are trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may not be mischaracterizing it, but I think I still think that your question was unnecessary --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- considering her previous answer. She started by saying, I don't know what report he is referring to, I haven't seen the report he is referring to; and then she refers to directly to the ICMP as being the source that she could -- as far as she could understand, and then she said, I don't know where he gets the numbers. And then you ask her, Does he identify it anywhere in his report. Well, I think you can move through --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Fair enough, Mr. President. I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me clarify. Dr. Komar, were you able to review the raw data on a spreadsheet form that was provided by the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: I was given a number of Excel spreadsheets that are identified as copies of ICMP data.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Looking at all the reports and the testimony that some, admittedly, predate and some post-date this November 2007 letter from Parsons, have you come to learn whether or not any such formal or informal report from ICMP exists in connection with the DNA-based identification relating to MNI?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: All I can speak to is what was provided to me, which can be summed up with the raw databases, this one-page statement or memo from Parsons, and I'm trying to think if there's anything else specifically from ICMP. Oh, the SOPs, standard operating procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll touch on that little later. Again, now, going back to where we were leading to, and that is looking and defining the matching rates or the matched success rates with the collection dates. In your report, you then use the term "representation" or "representative" rates. Can you just tell me how that fits in, if we are using match rates with collection rates, and forgive me for asking, but I was a little confused on that.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Okay. The report begins by identifying in completely acceptable, mathematical terms how he defines his matching rate, so he is essentially saying, of the samples we got, here are the ones we've been able to match, and produces a mathematical statement to that effect. Absolutely fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's a methodological way of -- process that he was conducting, correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Yes, and that's in the second paragraph. No complaint with that whatsoever. He then in the third paragraph says, If we assume that, and then he lays out a set of criteria that form the basis for the hypothesis that he is then going to formulate, and again, completely scientifically acceptable to establish your parameters and list, and in fact, you are required to list and identify the assumptions you are basing that on, but there seems to be sort of a transition from talking about a matching rate into this notion of representation and sampling strategy without sufficient evidence such that others can evaluate it how he makes that leap and that there is a disconnect between identifying a matching rate and then arguing that that in fact represents a collection rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Forgive me, Doctor. I'm not sure I fully understand. We will flush it out, but I think we'll need for all of our purposes if we can have 1D703 on the screen, and I know you have it in front of you, Doctor, and you were looking at it, so let's just take a look at that. Oh, I'm sorry. Please, this is under seal, I'm told, but I just want to double-check. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I couldn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was it lifted?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not yet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So we shouldn't broadcast it, either, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Registrar will look into that, okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are looking into the matter, Mr. Ostojic and Mr. Vanderpuye. I'm also told that 1D703 hasn't been tendered as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Has not been tendered?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It could well be the position, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'll look into that too. Can we maybe reference it, then, just by the date of the letter, and then we'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait, because it could have a duplicate number from what I can understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It has been tendered by someone else, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I understand that P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With a different reference number.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand it's P3005. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is under seal. It is under seal, so be careful, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And no broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, in examining and in formulating your opinions in this case, have you had an opportunity to review this document that erroneously I've been calling 1D703, which is actually P3005, dated the 30th of November, 2007, from Dr. Parsons?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In your report, again, in the first section, this is where you analyse and highlight some of the opinions that you have in connection with that?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you were in the process of explaining to us some of the methodology that was used and if you could be kind enough in the just a couple minutes that we have and we'll pick up on this topic in some detail tomorrow. You were referencing certain things in the report and just so we can have a better appreciation when you discuss matching rates with collection rates and then representation, just point out where we are gleaning that from?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: He defines and states his matching rate in the second paragraph and he defines that by taking the number of individual profiles that ICMP have been able to extract from the samples that were given to them, and he compares that to what he calls family matches or what are in essence positive identifications of missing individuals. So he takes the 5.280 individual profiles, those are simply DNA fingerprints, if you will, the physical profile that is created when the extraction occurs and the DNA is amplified and it's put out. And he compares that to what he calls family matches which are essentially identifications that stem from that based on a comparison of those profiles with reference samples provided by missing persons family members. So that is he how he defines his matching rate and that's completely appropriate, completely accurate. Doing that is appropriate. The confusion, the lack of clarity, the issue arises in the next paragraph when he defines what his assumptions are that allows him to make a further calculation using that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just -- I don't mean to interrupt you. We just have a minute left. I just wanted to ask you -- and you have it in your report the assumptions that he is using are -- in your opinion, or plainly as you stat in your report, incorrect?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR
utterances.text: Well, they are assumptions. The problem is -- the question is whether an assumption can ultimately render the conclusion invalid. Is the assumption so questionable that it can ultimately render the conclusion drawn from it invalid. I would suggest given the assumptions he defines and his bending or utilizing matching rates in lieu of representation would render the conclusion he draws from it questionable.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Komar. With your permission, Mr. President, if we could end here and then pick up tomorrow morning, I would appreciate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Ostojic. We stand adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
